title: Childhood (Poem, Hornbill)
tagline: Markus Natten’s repeated question — when did childhood end? — answered by geography, hypocrisy and independence of mind.

overview.intro: A poem that asks one question several times and refuses a comfortable answer. The speaker looks back at the moment he stopped being eleven, at his discovery that heaven and hell are not on any map, at the gap between what adults say and what they do, and finally at the recognition that he had acquired a mind of his own — after which childhood is looked for rather than lived. The unit studies the poem’s repetitive structure, its cataloguing of lost certainties, and the quiet symbol with which it closes.

learn.title: The repeated question and what it refuses

blocks.text: The poem is built on repetition: the same question returns at intervals, each time receiving a different candidate answer. That structure tells the reader two things before any content is absorbed. The first is that the speaker has no single explanation — childhood did not end in one dramatic hour, he believes, but in a series of small discoveries. The second is that the question matters more than its answers: he keeps asking because no answer satisfies, and the poem’s movement is from confident attempts at explanation toward the recognition that the loss cannot be dated.

The opening identification of himself as no longer eleven is deliberately flat, a fact rather than an event, and it sets the poem’s register: reflective, unadorned, argumentative rather than nostalgic. Unlike poems that mourn childhood through imagery, this one interrogates its ending through reasoning, which is itself a demonstration of the independence of mind that the poem finally identifies as childhood’s real executioner.

items: The question recurs, receiving a new candidate answer each time.
Repetition establishes that the loss cannot be dated to one hour.
The tone is argumentative rather than sentimental.
Each answer removes a different childhood certainty.
The reasoning voice is itself what the poem ends by diagnosing.

learn.title: Geography, hypocrisy and the failure of outside authority

blocks.text: The first substantive answer is intellectual: the speaker decided that heaven and hell must be wrong because geography, which he trusted, could not produce them. The scene is small and precise — a child reasoning that if a map does not contain what adults insist on, then either the map or the claim must fail — and the effect is the loss of an entire cosmology delivered as a homework correction. The poem treats this not as trauma but as a step: authority that cannot be verified stops being authority.

The second answer is moral. The speaker watches adults say one thing and do another, and the discovery that people’s words have parted from their actions strikes at trust rather than at belief. Together the two episodes mark a coherent double loss — the failure of outside authority in religion, and the failure of consistency in human beings — after which the only authority left is the speaker’s own judgement. That prepares the third answer, which the poem states plainly: the arrival of an independent mind, thinking for itself, is the event that finally makes childhood irrecoverable.

learn.title: The infant’s face: where childhood finally is

blocks.text: The closing movement does something different from the rest of the poem. After four attempts to date the ending, the speaker stops reasoning and reports where he finds childhood when he looks for it: in the face of a baby, where it is observed rather than possessed. The shift from argument to image is the poem’s structural turn, and it resolves the question by relocating the answer — childhood is not a period he can re-enter but a condition he can now only recognise in others.

The symbol is exact: infancy is the only stage at which the qualities the poem has lost — unreasoned trust, unbroken continuity between word and deed, a mind not yet split from the world — still exist together. There is also quiet irony in it: the man who has spent the poem thinking his way through the loss can only point at the answer rather than reclaim it. Answers on the ending should therefore connect it to the earlier stages — each quality lost is present in the infant — rather than treating the image as a generic sentimental close.

learn.title: Structure, tone and how the poem argues

blocks.text: The poem’s form is its argument. The repeated question divides the text into movements, each ending with a candidate answer that fails to close the enquiry, and the accumulation produces the sense of a mind testing and discarding explanations. The lines are conversational and largely unrhymed in effect, which suits a speaker reasoning aloud rather than declaiming, and the absence of ornate imagery keeps the reader’s attention on the logic of each discovery.

The tone deserves particular care in answers: the poem is wistful but not self-pitying, critical of adults but not bitter, and its final resignation is composed rather than defeated. That tonal control is achieved by keeping the personal out of the catalogue — no scene of cruelty, no dramatic break — so that childhood ends quietly, in a series of ordinary realisations. For extract questions: identify which candidate answer the quoted lines belong to, what certainty each removes, and how the accumulation prepares the closing image.

questions.prompt: What four candidate answers does the poem give for the end of childhood?
questions.answer: The four are: reaching the age at which he was no longer eleven, a plain fact rather than an event; the discovery that geography cannot produce heaven or hell, which removes outside religious authority; the recognition that adults say one thing and do another, which removes trust in people; and the arrival of an independent mind, thinking for itself, which removes the capacity to remain childlike. The poem offers each in turn and closes by locating childhood in an infant’s face instead of dating its loss.
questions.explanation: All four candidates in order, with what each removes, are required.

questions.prompt: What is the significance of the poem’s repeated question?
questions.answer: The repetition divides the poem into movements, each supplying a fresh candidate answer, and its recurrence after every failed explanation tells the reader that no answer will settle the matter — the enquiry outlives its solutions. The refrain also measures the speaker’s state of mind: he reasons, discards and reasons again, which is precisely the independent thinking the poem finally names as childhood’s executioner, so the structure enacts its own subject. Finally, the repeated question keeps the tone wistful rather than despairing: the speaker is still asking because the loss still matters, and that persistence converts a catalogue of grievances into a sustained reflection.
questions.explanation: Three functions are required: structural division, the demonstration of independent thought, and the maintenance of wistful persistence rather than despair.

questions.prompt: How does the poem move from reasoning to image? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: The poem spends most of its length reasoning and closes by looking. Its first three movements are arguments: the speaker states a date (no longer eleven), tests a claim against a trusted authority (geography cannot yield heaven and hell), and observes a contradiction in human behaviour (adults say one thing and do another), and each test returns a result that removes a certainty rather than an event. The fourth movement turns the method on itself: the speaker recognises that the mind doing this testing is precisely what ended childhood, so the instrument of enquiry becomes its own explanation, and the reasoning voice demonstrates the very independence it names. At that point argument has exhausted itself — there is nothing further to deduce — and the poem changes register, relocating childhood from the speaker’s past to the face of an infant. The image works because everything the reasoning established is present in it: the baby has not yet divided word from deed, has no authority to doubt, and does not yet think apart from the world, so the infant embodies the condition the catalogue described as lost. The resolution is therefore not a fifth candidate answer but a change of category: childhood is redefined as something observable rather than recoverable, which is why the poem can end in quiet recognition instead of another question. An answer should quote from three of the four movements and show how the final image completes rather than contradicts them, because the strength of the poem is that its feeling arrives only after its logic has finished.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the four movements traced with quotations, the observation that the reasoning voice enacts its own diagnosis, and the argument that the closing image completes the catalogue rather than replacing it.

questions.prompt: Does the poem blame adults for the loss of childhood, or is the loss presented as natural? Discuss.
questions.answer: The case for blame rests on the poem’s second discovery and its tone. The speaker’s sharpest observation is about grown people: they say one thing and do another, and the discovery is presented as a wound to trust rather than as an innocent mistake. The same watchfulness runs through the poem’s treatment of religion — heaven and hell are inherited claims that adult authority repeats and that collapse under a child’s checking — so adults appear as the custodians who failed: they transmitted beliefs they had not examined and standards they did not keep. The poem’s persistent questioning can also be read as the residue of that failure: he asks when childhood ended because the answers he was given were never trustworthy in the first place. The case for a natural loss rests on the structure and on the poem’s restraint. The four candidates are not tragedies — a birthday, a map, an observation, a capacity — and none involves cruelty, loss of loved ones or misfortune; childhood ends through ordinary maturation, the normal operation of reason, and the arrival of an independent mind, which the poem presents as an achievement as much as a cost. The closing image reinforces the natural reading: infancy is simply an earlier stage, and the speaker’s calm in pointing at it suggests acceptance rather than accusation — he does not resent the baby, he recognises a phase. Even the hypocrisy discovery is stated without a villain; no particular adult is condemned, and the judgement is general and observational. The balanced judgement is that the poem holds both: adults supply the specific failures that make the loss painful, while the loss itself is inevitable and would have occurred had they been perfect, because reason and independence arrive by the same route either way. The best answers will separate what made the loss painful from what made it inevitable, since the poem’s distinction between those two is what keeps it wistful rather than angry.
questions.explanation: Full marks require both cases with evidence, the separation of pain from inevitability, and a judgement about the tone as evidence for the poem’s position.
